entities.summary:
Sancha of Majorca (c. 1285 – 28 July 1345), Queen consort of Naples and Jerusalem, became a pivotal figure in the political and religious life of Southern Italy during the first half of the 14th century through her marriage to Robert the Wise, King of Naples. A member of the House of Barcelona and daughter of King James II of Majorca, Sancha brought significant dynastic connections to the Angevin court, solidifying alliances and influencing the cultural and spiritual landscape of one of Europe's most powerful kingdoms. Her deep devotion to the Franciscan Order, particularly the Spiritual Franciscans, shaped royal patronage and introduced a unique ascetic fervor into the Neapolitan monarchy, making her a queen whose piety was as notable as her political acumen.

Elevated to queen consort upon Robert's accession in 1309, Sancha actively participated in court life and exerted considerable influence over her husband, particularly in matters of religious policy and intellectual patronage. She fostered a vibrant intellectual environment, attracting scholars and theologians to Naples, and was a staunch patron of the Franciscan friars, commissioning churches and convents. Her political significance was further cemented following Robert's death in 1343, when she assumed the regency for her young step-granddaughter, Joanna I of Naples. During her brief regency, Sancha navigated a complex political landscape marked by internal factionalism and external pressures from the papacy and other European powers, striving to secure the succession and maintain stability in the volatile Kingdom of Naples.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sancha of Majorca significantly influenced the religious and political landscape of the Kingdom of Naples as queen consort and regent, notably shaping Franciscan patronage and providing transitional leadership during a critical succession. Her personal piety and eventual abdication left a unique mark on the era's understanding of royal duty and spiritual devotion.
